title: Short Stuff: History of OK
summary: Short Stuff episode on the origin and usage of the word "okay." Josh and Chuck (with Speaker 2 reading material) describe the word's versatility as adjective, interjection, verb and noun. They trace its origin to 1838-1839 Boston and New York penny press culture: an abbreviation craze started by Charles Gordon Green, editor of Boston's Morning Post; a trend of purposeful misspellings (e.g., KG for "no go," OW for "all right"); and the March 23, 1839 "O.K." coined by Green as a joke abbreviation of "all correct," in a exchange with the Providence Journal editor over the Anti-Bell-Ringing Society. The term was popularized by Martin Van Buren's 1840 campaign slogan "Old Kinderhook," which made "OK" mean "all is okay." Linguists Allan Metcalf and Anatoly Liberman are cited, with Metcalf describing OK as a neutral affirmative. The episode closes with style guide differences (AP, Chicago Manual of Style, Grammarly) on capitalization and periods, and a note on lowercase "okay" versus "OK."

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Short Stuff episode with Chuck and Jerry standing in, and the hosts say okay is one of the most versatile words in English.

segments.title: Versatility of the word okay
segments.summary: The hosts and Speaker 2 go through okay as an adjective, interjection, verb and noun, with jokey examples.

segments.title: Alan Walker Reed and the origin research
segments.summary: The hosts credit etymologist Alan Walker Reed, who in the 1960s traced the origin of OK through old-fashioned research.

segments.title: 1838 abbreviation craze in penny papers
segments.summary: In the late 1830s, cheap penny press papers fueled a craze for abbreviations, starting in Boston in summer 1838 with Charles Gordon Green of the Morning Post, spreading to New York and elsewhere. Examples include GTDHD and WYG.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the next part of the story.

segments.title: Misspelling trend and KG, OW
segments.summary: A parallel trend of purposeful misspellings in penny papers produced abbreviations such as KG for no go, KY for no use, and OW for all right. Listeners sometimes mistype SYSK.

segments.title: March 1839 birth of O.K.
segments.summary: Anatoly Liberman's research pinpointed March 23, 1839. Green wrote 'all correct' as 'O K' in a exchange with the Providence Journal editor over the Anti-Bell-Ringing Society.

segments.title: Old Kinderhook and the neutral affirmative
segments.summary: Martin Van Buren's 1840 campaign nickname Old Kinderhook made okay a slogan. Van Buren lost to William Henry Harrison. Metcalf described OK as a neutral affirmative.

segments.title: Style guides and capitalization
segments.summary: AP uses uppercase OK without periods; Chicago Manual of Style allows both; Grammarly data shows uppercase about a third of the time in edited writing. The hosts discuss lowercase okay.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing banter about listener mail on the etymology joke, and the iHeartRadio production credit.
